topic: Project Orrery: A Portable Codex Skill for Traceable Project Docs

key_points: AGENTS.md is an open format for guiding coding agents, used by 60k+ open-source projects
Positioned as 'a README for agents' — a dedicated, predictable place for agent context and instructions
Kept separate from README.md so human docs stay concise; one AGENTS.md works across Codex, Jules, Factory, Aider, goose, opencode, Zed, Warp, VS Code, Devin
Complements rather than replaces existing docs; predictable location for build steps, tests, conventions
Vercel's evals found a compressed 8KB docs index embedded in AGENTS.md achieved 100% pass rate, while skills maxed out at 79%
Skills were never invoked in 56% of eval cases; adding a skill produced zero improvement over baseline (53% vs 53%)
An unused skill in the environment can introduce noise/distraction (performed worse on some test metrics)
AGENTS.md provides persistent context on every turn without the agent needing to decide to load it — key advantage over on-demand skills
Skills are the authoring format for reusable workflows in ChatGPT and Codex, built on the open agent skills standard (agentskills.io)
A skill is a directory with SKILL.md (required name+description) plus optional scripts/, references/, assets/, agents/
Uses progressive disclosure: starts with name+description, loads full SKILL.md only when the agent decides to use it
Skills list budget capped at ~2% of context window or 8000 chars; large skill sets may be omitted with a warning
ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a well-established pattern for capturing decisions and their rationale
Provides templates and examples for software planning and IT leadership
ADRs are the foundation Orrery builds on — append-only decision history is a core authority layer
Shows the broader ecosystem of decision documentation that predates AI agents
Documentation-as-code treats docs as versioned, reviewable artifacts in the repo
Principles: docs live with code, are versioned, reviewed, and tested
Challenges include keeping docs in sync with code and avoiding drift
Relevant context for why AI-assisted repos need stronger traceability than plain docs-as-code
Daemons pivoted from building agents to 'cleaning up after them' — evidence of the documentation-drift problem
AI agents produce source and docs faster than their purpose, authority, and relationships can be understood
Frames the pain point Orrery directly addresses: losing control of a codebase to fast agent output
Validates the market need for traceability and observability tooling around agent work

stats.fact: AGENTS.md open format is used by over 60,000 open-source projects
Vercel evals: an 8KB docs index in AGENTS.md achieved a 100% pass rate vs skills maxing out at 79%
In Vercel's evals, skills were never invoked in 56% of cases and produced zero improvement over baseline (53% vs 53%)
Codex caps the initial skills list at ~2% of the model's context window, or 8,000 characters when the window is unknown
Project Orrery (ItIsMixian/Orrery) is an MIT-licensed, platform-neutral project with 47 GitHub stars, created 2026-08-17
Orrery v0.2.0 is the first public release; Codex integration is 'verified' on Codex Desktop 26.818.2441.0 / codex-cli 0.148.0-alpha.21
Orrery ships adapters for Codex (verified), Claude Code (experimental), DeepSeek Harness (experimental), and Harness JSON (experimental)

angles: The core governing rule 'accepted does not mean implemented, and planned does not mean proven' — an authority model that prevents AI docs drift
Portable skill vs platform lock-in: one portable skill with thin adapters for Codex, Claude Code, and DeepSeek Harness
Bridging the AGENTS.md-vs-skills debate (Vercel's finding) — Orrery uses AGENTS.md as the authority entrance AND a skill as the delivery layer
Separating reader-specific entrances (agents vs humans) without splitting the single source of truth
Local observatory / project memory: turning document growth into a project-level instrument panel with dashboard, roadmap, health, trend views
Safe, non-destructive adoption: dry-run scaffolding, create-only defaults, strict allowlist upgrades with backups
Solving the 'losing control of a codebase to fast agent output' problem that tools like Daemons are also chasing
